Latent and species embeddings

Source: vignettes/articles/embeddings.Rmd
embeddings.Rmd

A trained RESOLVE model holds three kinds of learned vectors, called embeddings: one per plot, one per species, and one per genus and per family. The plot vector is the model’s summary of a plot, from which it predicts every target. The species, genus and family vectors are the rows of the tables the model looks species up in.

This article covers getting each kind out of a trained model, projecting the plot vectors onto two axes to look at them, comparing species and genera by their vectors, which encodings keep the effect of each species separate, finding similar and unusual plots and reading gradients from the vectors, and computing plot vectors from the encoded inputs directly.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/resolve/r")

# The engine library, downloaded once
library(resolveR)
resolve.install_backend()
pip install resolve-core

A model to read

The examples use the survey of 150 plots in the Alps that ships with the R package: plots with one row per plot (coordinates, elevation in metres, habitat) and species with one row per species recorded on a plot (genus, family, cover in percent). The model predicts elevation and habitat from the species alone.

The encoding is how the model turns a plot’s species list into numbers. The rank-pool encoding used here gives every species its own row in one table and averages the rows of a plot’s species, weighted by their cover, so it has a species table to read. Encoding the species set compares the encodings.

plots <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "plots.csv", package = "resolveR"))
species <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "species.csv", package = "resolveR"))

dataset <- resolve.dataset.frame(
  plots, species,
  roles = list(plot_id = "plot_id", species_id = "species",
               abundance = "cover", genus = "genus", family = "family"),
  targets = list(
    elevation = list(column = "elevation", task = "regression"),
    habitat = list(column = "habitat", task = "classification")
  ),
  config = list(species_encoding = "rank_pool")
)
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "rank_pool.pt")
fit <- resolve.train.dataset(dataset, maxEpochs = 100L,
                             savePath = path, verbose = FALSE)
predictor <- resolve.load(path)
import os
import tempfile

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import resolve_core as rc

data = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gcol33/resolve/master/r/inst/extdata/"
plots = pd.read_csv(data + "plots.csv")
species = pd.read_csv(data + "species.csv")

roles = rc.RoleMapping()
roles.plot_id = "plot_id"
roles.species_id = "species"
roles.abundance = "cover"
roles.genus = "genus"
roles.family = "family"
targets = [rc.TargetSpec.regression("elevation"),
           rc.TargetSpec.classification("habitat", 4)]
config = rc.DatasetConfig()
config.species_encoding = rc.SpeciesEncodingMode.RankPool
dataset = rc.ResolveDataset.from_pandas(plots, species, roles, targets, config)

model = rc.ResolveModel(dataset.schema, rc.model_config_for_dataset(dataset))
train_config = rc.TrainConfig()
train_config.max_epochs = 100
trainer = rc.Trainer(model, train_config)
trainer.prepare_data(dataset)
result = trainer.fit()

path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "rank_pool.pt")
trainer.save(path)
predictor = rc.Predictor.load(path)

Plot embeddings

The model’s encoder turns a plot’s species composition, and its coordinates and covariates when it has them, into one vector, the plot’s latent representation. Each target has a head, a small network that reads its prediction off that vector. Predicting with the latent representation switched on returns it, one row per plot, in the dataset’s plot order.

out <- resolve.predict.dataset(predictor, dataset, returnLatent = TRUE)
latent <- out$latent
dim(latent)
#> [1] 150  64
tail(predictor$model_config()$hidden_dims, 1)
#> [1] 64
out = predictor.predict_dataset(dataset, return_latent=True)
latent = out.latent.numpy()
latent.shape
#> (150, 64)
predictor.model.latent_dim
#> 64

The vector is as wide as the encoder’s last hidden layer. Every head reads the same vector, so two plots close together in the latent space are plots the model expects to have similar values on every target at once.

Projecting the latent space

Sixty-four numbers per plot cannot be drawn directly. Principal component analysis finds the directions along which the plot vectors vary most; the first two give a map of the plots in which distances approximate those in the latent space. The habitat is taken from plots by plot identifier, since the result follows the dataset’s plot order.

pcs <- prcomp(latent)
habitat <- factor(plots$habitat[match(out$plot_ids, plots$plot_id)])
colours <- c("#E69F00", "#0072B2", "#009E73", "#CC79A7")
shapes <- c(16, 17, 15, 18)

par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
plot(pcs$x[, 1], pcs$x[, 2], col = colours[habitat], pch = shapes[habitat],
     xlab = "Principal component 1", ylab = "Principal component 2")
legend("top", legend = levels(habitat), col = colours, pch = shapes,
       horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", inset = c(0, -0.14), xpd = TRUE)

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

centred = latent - latent.mean(axis=0)
u, s, vt = np.linalg.svd(centred, full_matrices=False)
pcs = centred @ vt.T
habitat = pd.Series(out.plot_ids).map(plots.set_index("plot_id").habitat)

colours = ["#E69F00", "#0072B2", "#009E73", "#CC79A7"]
shapes = ["o", "^", "s", "D"]
plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 13
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))
for name, colour, shape in zip(sorted(habitat.unique()), colours, shapes):
    rows = (habitat == name).to_numpy()
    ax.scatter(pcs[rows, 0], pcs[rows, 1], c=colour, marker=shape, label=name)
ax.set_xlabel("Principal component 1");
ax.set_ylabel("Principal component 2");
ax.legend(ncol=4, loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.0), frameon=False);
fig.tight_layout()

Plots of one habitat mostly fall together, because the habitat head is trained to tell them apart from the same vectors. The signs of the components are arbitrary, so the map can come out mirrored between runs. Non-linear projections such as UMAP (uniform manifold approximation and projection) or t-SNE (t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding) take the same matrix as input.

Species embeddings

The species table has one row per species in the vocabulary, the list of species the model was trained with, in the same order. Row 1 in R and row 0 in Python is the reserved unknown entry: every species outside the vocabulary is looked up there.

species_table <- predictor$get_species_embeddings()
species_names <- predictor$species_vocab()
dim(species_table)
#> [1] 26 32
head(species_names, 4)
#> [1] "<UNK>"               "Acer pseudoplatanus" "Silene acaulis"     
#> [4] "Abies alba"
species_table = predictor.get_species_embeddings().numpy()
species_names = list(predictor.species_vocab)
species_table.shape
#> (26, 32)
species_names[:4]
#> ['<UNK>', 'Acer pseudoplatanus', 'Silene acaulis', 'Abies alba']

The encodings that keep a row per species return a table: embed, rank pool and transformer. Under the embed encoding each rank position, from the most to the least abundant species of a plot, has its own region of the table, and the vector returned for a species is the average over the positions. The hash encoding computes a species’ contribution from its name and has no table; the sparse encoding gives a species its own column in the weights of the first layer. Both return NULL in R and None in Python.

Taxonomy embeddings

With a genus or family column among the roles, every encoding also learns a table per taxonomic level. Both tables reserve their first row for the unknown entry too.

genus_table <- predictor$get_genus_embeddings()
genus_names <- predictor$genus_vocab()
dim(genus_table)
#> [1] 23  8
dim(predictor$get_family_embeddings())
#> [1] 11  8
head(genus_names, 4)
#> [1] "<UNK>"         "Abies"         "Acer"          "Arrhenatherum"
genus_table = predictor.get_genus_embeddings().numpy()
genus_names = list(predictor.genus_vocab)
genus_table.shape
#> (23, 8)
predictor.get_family_embeddings().shape
#> torch.Size([11, 8])
genus_names[:4]
#> ['<UNK>', 'Abies', 'Acer', 'Arrhenatherum']

A dataset carries the same vocabularies, so the names are available without a checkpoint.

head(dataset$schema()$genus_vocab, 4)
#> [1] "<UNK>"         "Abies"         "Acer"          "Arrhenatherum"
head(dataset$species_vocab(), 4)
#> [1] "<UNK>"               "Acer pseudoplatanus" "Silene acaulis"     
#> [4] "Abies alba"
dataset.schema.genus_vocab[:4]
#> ['<UNK>', 'Abies', 'Acer', 'Arrhenatherum']
dataset.species_vocab[:4]
#> ['<UNK>', 'Acer pseudoplatanus', 'Silene acaulis', 'Abies alba']

Comparing species and genera

The cosine similarity of two vectors is 1 when they point the same way, 0 when they are unrelated and -1 when they point in opposite directions. Computed between all rows of the genus table, leaving out the unknown entry, it lists the genera whose vectors are closest to a chosen one.

cosine <- function(x) {
  unit <- x / sqrt(rowSums(x^2))
  unit %*% t(unit)
}
genera <- genus_table[-1, ]
rownames(genera) <- genus_names[-1]
similarity <- cosine(genera)
round(sort(similarity["Quercus", ], decreasing = TRUE)[2:6], 3)
#> Sesleria     Acer    Abies    Salix    Larix 
#>    0.585    0.460    0.421    0.343    0.298
def cosine(x):
    unit = x / np.linalg.norm(x, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return unit @ unit.T

genera = pd.DataFrame(genus_table[1:], index=genus_names[1:])
similarity = pd.DataFrame(cosine(genera.to_numpy()),
                          index=genera.index, columns=genera.index)
similarity["Quercus"].drop("Quercus").sort_values(ascending=False).head(5).round(3)
#> Eriophorum    0.489
#> Abies         0.389
#> Salix         0.381
#> Carex         0.311
#> Trifolium     0.292
#> Name: Quercus, dtype: float32

Two genera end up close when the model found them interchangeable for predicting its targets on this dataset. That can match ecological or phylogenetic similarity, and it measures neither.

The same table clusters hierarchically. Ward’s method joins, at each step, the two groups whose merger adds the least within-group variance.

tree <- hclust(dist(genera), method = "ward.D2")
par(mar = c(4.5, 1, 1, 9))
plot(as.dendrogram(tree), horiz = TRUE, xlab = "Height")

from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage

tree = linkage(genera.to_numpy(), method="ward")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 6))
dendrogram(tree, labels=list(genera.index), orientation="left", ax=ax,
           leaf_font_size=13,
           color_threshold=0, above_threshold_color="black");
ax.set_xlabel("Height");
fig.tight_layout()

The species table compares the same way.

known <- species_table[-1, ]
rownames(known) <- species_names[-1]
round(sort(cosine(known)["Carex curvula", ], decreasing = TRUE)[2:4], 3)
#>   Acer pseudoplatanus Arrhenatherum elatius          Pinus cembra 
#>                 0.360                 0.287                 0.198
known = species_table[1:]
names = pd.Index(species_names[1:])
row = cosine(known)[names.get_loc("Carex curvula")]
pd.Series(row, index=names).drop("Carex curvula").nlargest(3).round(3)
#> Festuca rubra       0.333
#> Quercus petraea     0.299
#> Caltha palustris    0.293
#> dtype: float32

Linear pooling and what stays readable

Several encodings combine the species of a plot linearly before any non-linear layer mixes them:

  • hash adds each species’ cover, with a sign of +1 or -1, to the column its name hashes to, so a plot’s hashed vector is a signed sum of one term per species;
  • rank pool takes the cover-weighted mean of the species’ rows;
  • sparse passes the plot’s vector of species covers to a linear layer, which adds one column of weights per species.

In these three, the input to the encoder is a sum of one term per species, so it splits into the contribution of each species. The split holds up to the first non-linear layer; after it, the encoder mixes the terms. The transformer encoding gives up the split on purpose: attention lets the effect of a species depend on the other species of the plot, which is what it is used for.

Practical uses

Similar plots

The plots most similar to a given one are those whose latent vectors have the highest cosine similarity to its vector.

rownames(latent) <- out$plot_ids
plot_similarity <- cosine(latent)
round(sort(plot_similarity["A001", ], decreasing = TRUE)[2:6], 3)
#>  A015  A149  A063  A121  A134 
#> 0.998 0.996 0.995 0.995 0.994
plot_similarity = pd.DataFrame(cosine(latent), index=out.plot_ids,
                               columns=out.plot_ids)
plot_similarity["A001"].drop("A001").nlargest(5).round(3)
#> A063    0.997
#> A149    0.996
#> A015    0.995
#> A121    0.995
#> A045    0.995
#> Name: A001, dtype: float32

Predicting new plots shows retrieval, which blends a prediction with the recorded values of the most similar training plots.

Unusual plots

A plot whose nearest neighbours are all far from it has a composition unlike the others the model saw. The mean similarity to its five nearest neighbours ranks the plots by how isolated they are.

nearest <- apply(plot_similarity, 1, function(s) mean(sort(s, decreasing = TRUE)[2:6]))
round(sort(nearest)[1:5], 3)
#>  A048  A145  A082  A122  A096 
#> 0.713 0.770 0.794 0.804 0.805
nearest = plot_similarity.apply(lambda s: s.nlargest(6).iloc[1:].mean())
nearest.nsmallest(5).round(3)
#> A140    0.791
#> A067    0.807
#> A096    0.808
#> A082    0.810
#> A145    0.826
#> dtype: float32

Read an isolated plot next to its prediction error before calling it an outlier: it may be rare in the survey and still well predicted.

Gradients

The share of the variance each principal component explains shows how many directions the latent space mainly uses. A component that correlates with a target is a gradient along that target.

round(summary(pcs)$importance["Proportion of Variance", 1:3], 3)
#>   PC1   PC2   PC3 
#> 0.378 0.288 0.183
elevation <- plots$elevation[match(out$plot_ids, plots$plot_id)]
round(cor(pcs$x[, 1:3], elevation)[, 1], 3)
#>    PC1    PC2    PC3 
#> -0.774  0.205 -0.017
np.round(s[:3] ** 2 / np.sum(s ** 2), 3)
#> array([0.37 , 0.294, 0.148], dtype=float32)
elevation = pd.Series(out.plot_ids).map(plots.set_index("plot_id").elevation)
[round(np.corrcoef(pcs[:, i], elevation)[0, 1], 3) for i in range(3)]
#> [np.float64(-0.747), np.float64(-0.259), np.float64(-0.29)]

Embeddings from the encoded inputs

A predictor also computes the latent vectors from the encoded inputs directly, the tensors a dataset holds, which is what a custom analysis on modified inputs needs. It assembles and standardises the inputs as training did, so the result equals the latent representation from prediction.

inputs = dict(unknown_fraction=dataset.unknown_fraction,
              species_ids=dataset.species_ids,
              pool_genus_ids=dataset.pool_genus_ids,
              pool_family_ids=dataset.pool_family_ids,
              pool_weights=dataset.pool_weights,
              pool_mask=dataset.pool_mask,
              pool_has_cover=dataset.pool_has_cover)
direct = predictor.get_embeddings(**inputs)
direct.equal(out.latent)

Each input is a keyword, and inputs the encoding does not read are left out. ResolveModel.get_latent() runs the encoder of a model you hold, such as trainer.model in a custom training loop, on the same inputs, with the continuous block (coordinates, covariates, the unknown-species columns and, under the hash encoding, the hash vector) already assembled and standardised. The model’s tables are read the same way, before or after training:

trainer.model.get_species_weights().shape
trainer.model.get_genus_weights().shape

In R, predictor$get_embeddings() takes the encoded inputs as positional arguments only, and a fit does not return its model, so this route is shown in Python.
